text: Antonio Negri (/ˈnɛɡri/; Italian: [ˈneːɡri]; 1 August 1933 – 16 December 2023) was an Italian political philosopher renowned as one of the most prominent theorists of autonomism and co-author of the books *Empire* and *Multitude: War and Democracy in the Age of Empire* with Michael Hardt. Born in Padua, in the Veneto region of northeastern Italy, Negri’s father was a communist militant from Bologna in Emilia-Romagna, and although he died when Negri was two, his political engagement influenced Negri’s early exposure to Marxism; his mother was a teacher from Poggio Rusco in Lombardy. Negri began his activism in the 1950s with the Roman Catholic youth organization Gioventù Italiana di Azione Cattolica (GIAC), joined the Italian Socialist Party in 1956, and became a communist in 1955 while working at the Nahsonim kibbutz in central Israel, a Jewish communist community based on Zionist socialism. He earned a doctorate in philosophy in 1956 and was hired as a professor of dottrina dello Stato ("state doctrine"), a field akin to the philosophy of law, at the University of Padua, where he taught state and constitutional theory. In the early 1960s, he joined the editorial group of *Quaderni Rossi*, a journal that marked the intellectual revival of Marxism outside the Communist Party. In 1969, he co-founded the Potere Operaio (Worker Power) group with Oreste Scalzone and Franco Piperno, launching the operaismo (workerism) movement. On 16 March 1978, former Italian prime minister Aldo Moro was kidnapped in Rome by the Red Brigades (Brigate Rosse or BR), and nine days before his death, the BR called Moro’s family to inform them of his impending death—this call was later revealed to have been made by Valerio Morucci, not Negri. On 7 April 1979, Negri was arrested and charged with kidnapping, assassination, and insurrection, including leadership of the Red Brigades, masterminding the 1978 kidnapping and murder of Aldo Moro, and plotting to overthrow the government. While a leader of the BR testified that Negri had nothing to do with the group, charges such as "armed insurrection against the state" were dropped, but he was sentenced in absentia to 30 years in prison in 1984 after fleeing to France, with an additional four years for moral responsibility for political violence in the 1960s and 1970s, specifically for instigating the murder of Carlo Saronio and for "morally concurred" involvement in the murder of Andrea Lombardini during a failed bank robbery. Michel Foucault remarked, "Isn't he in jail simply for being an intellectual?" and French philosophers Félix Guattari and Gilles Deleuze signed *L'Appel des intellectuels français contre la répression en Italie* in 1977 in protest against Negri’s imprisonment. Italian President Francesco Cossiga described Negri as "a psychopath" who "poisoned the minds of an entire generation of Italy's youth." In 1983, while still in prison, Negri was elected to the Italian legislature as a member of the Radical Party, used parliamentary immunity to be freed, and fled to France with the help of Félix Guattari and Amnesty International, though his immunity was later revoked by the Chamber of Deputies. Protected by the Mitterrand doctrine, he taught at Paris VIII (Vincennes) and the Collège international de philosophie, alongside Jacques Derrida, Michel Foucault, and Gilles Deleuze. In 1997, after a plea-bargain that reduced his sentence from 30 to 13 years, he returned to Italy to serve the remainder of his sentence, during which time he wrote many of his most influential works. He was released in 2003 and lived in Venice and Paris with his partner, the French philosopher Judith Revel. He was the father of film director Anna Negri. Negri was a central theorist of autonomist Marxism and a prominent figure in libertarian socialism, communism, and Marxism. In *Empire*, co-authored with Michael Hardt, they ask how labor, with its life-affirming potential, has become a tool of capitalist discipline, exploitation, and domination, and they critique liberal and socialist notions of labor and institutional reform from a radical democratic perspective, challenging the state-form itself. They argue that the rise of "Empire" marks the end of national conflict, where the enemy is no longer ideological or national but is instead a criminal threatening the law, and is both "banalized" and "absolutized." Empire is constituted by a monarchy (the United States and G8, and institutions like NATO, IMF, WTO), an oligarchy (multinational corporations and nation-states), and a democracy (NGOs and the UN). The book asserts that resistance to Empire is only possible through negation—“the will to be against”—and that although Empire is total, economic inequality persists and the identity of the poor endures. *Multitude* picks up where *Empire* leaves off, analyzing war and its contradictions, and focusing on the multitude and democracy. It is presented as a reiteration from a new point of view in a more accessible style, remaining a philosophical work aimed at shaping a conceptual ground for democratic political processes rather than offering a concrete program. In 2009, Negri completed *Commonwealth*, the final book in a trilogy beginning with *Empire* and continuing with *Multitude* in 2004. In *Commonwealth*, the authors introduce the concept of "the republic of property," stating that property remains the foundation of every modern political constitution. Part two explores altermodernity, which involves breaking with the fixed dialectic between modern sovereignty and antimodern resistance, transforming tradition, identity, and resistance into new forms. They argue that communism is defined by the common, capitalism by the private, and socialism (identified with statism) by the public. Alex Callinicos notes that the "common" includes not only natural resources but also languages, social practices, and modes of sociality, which are both means and results of biopolitical production. David Harvey observes that Hardt and Negri seek an altermodernity outside the binary of modernity and anti-modernity, proposing a new form of communism that operates beyond the choice between capitalism and socialism, and that revolutionary thought must engage identity politics as the primary vehicle for struggle against the "republic of property." In a discussion with Harvey, Hardt and Negri clarify that singularity refers to a multiplicity of others, internal division, and a process of becoming over time. After *Commonwealth*, Negri wrote articles on the Arab Spring and Occupy movements. In May 2012, he self-published (with Michael Hardt) an electronic pamphlet titled *Declaration*, arguing that the Occupy and encampment movements explore new forms of democracy; the introduction was published at Jacobin under the title "Take Up the Baton." In October 2011, he and Hardt published an article in *Foreign Affairs* titled "The Encampment in Lower Manhattan Speaks to a Failure of Representation." In 2013, Negri published *Spinoza: Politics and Postmodernity*, a collection of essays on Spinoza and his contemporary relevance, translated by William McCuaig. In 2017, Negri and Michael Hardt published *Assembly*, which reflects on contemporary capitalism and social movements, drawing on concepts from their Empire trilogy such as the common, the multitude, and globalization. It introduces the concept of "assembly," inspired by Deleuze and Guattari’s "assemblage," as a way of understanding mass movements and constituent power. The book analyzes events since *Commonwealth* was published in 2009, including the rise of right-wing populism, Occupy Wall Street, automation, and the digital economy. It proposes that leadership in movements should serve specific, tactical, and short-term ends, while the multitude (or collective) articulates long-term goals to which leadership must submit. The book received generally positive reviews, with Kyle Perry arguing that advocates for a democratic world must embrace leadership, strategizing, and institution-building, and that new institutions should be "nonsovereign" and foster continuity and organization. Terence Renaud notes that while much of Hardt and Negri’s project may appear exhausted given the changed political terrain, they effectively highlight the internal challenges facing a resurgent left, such as sectarianism, heavy-handed leadership, and complacency, and insist on a self-critical, internally democratic left. Between 2016 and 2019, Negri published a three-volume collection of essays, translated and compiled into English. The first volume, *Marx and Foucault*, was published on 16 December 2016, in which he aims to show how the thinking of Marx and Foucault was synthesized into an original theoretical framework.

Terence Renaud, writing for the Los Angeles Review of Books, notes that given the significant changes in the political landscape since the publication of Empire in 2000, much of Hardt and Negri's project now appears to have concluded its contribution. Nevertheless, the authors effectively highlight the internal challenges a resurgent left faces, such as degenerating into sectarian conflict, authoritarian leadership, and complacency in its self-perception. Hardt and Negri advocate for a self-critical and internally democratic left that continuously questions its own assumptions, emphasizing that to transform society, the left must first transform itself. Between 2016 and 2019, Negri published a three-volume collection of essays translated and compiled into English. The first volume, Marx and Foucault, was released on 16 December 2016, aiming to demonstrate how Marx and Foucault's thought were synthesized, particularly in the context of Italy from May '68 onward. The second volume, From the Factory to the Metropolis, published in February 2018, analyzes the shift from the traditional industrial proletarian 'mass worker' to the contemporary 'socialised worker' and examines the modern 'metropolis' as a space of antagonism between finance capital (operating through rents) and the 'cognitive proletariat,' with the central question being how the 'common' of the latter can be mobilized to destroy capitalism. The third volume, Spinoza: Then and Now, published in February 2020, explores how Spinoza's thought represents a radical departure from past ideas and serves as a vital tool for envisioning politics beyond capitalism. On 29 October 2021, Negri released the first volume of a new trilogy, Marx in Movement: Operaismo in Context, which provides an account of the history of Italian Autonomist (or 'Autonomist Marxist') thought, especially focusing on Negri's development of the concept of the 'social worker' as a way to update Marxism in response to changes since Marx's era of factory-based labor. Negri married Paola Meo in 1962; they had two children, Anna and Francesco, and later divorced. He has another daughter, Nina Negri, from a separate relationship. He met the philosopher Judith Revel in 1996 and married her in 2016. Negri died in Paris on 16 December 2023, at the age of 90. The works listed in order of their first publication in English are: Transcendence, Spirituality, Practices, Immanence: A Conversation with Antonio Negri by Judith Revel, published in Rethinking Marxism, 28(3–4), 470–478 (2016).
